subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The 'chivalry thesis' in the sociology of gender and crime claims that:
options: Women commit more crime than official statistics show
Men commit no crime against women
Women are biologically incapable of crime
The criminal justice system treats women more leniently than men
questions.explain: The chivalry thesis suggests that a male-dominated justice system treats female offenders more leniently, lowering recorded female crime.

questions.q: In assessing documents as a secondary source, Scott's four criteria are authenticity, credibility, representativeness and:
options: Meaning
Falsifiability
Reliability
Cost
questions.explain: John Scott proposed judging documents by authenticity, credibility, representativeness and meaning (their interpretation and significance).

questions.q: Right realists such as Wilson and Herrnstein explain crime mainly through:
options: Rational choice, biological factors and inadequate socialisation
Capitalist exploitation of the proletariat
The deviancy amplification spiral
The chivalry of the courts
questions.explain: Right realists see crime as a rational choice influenced by individual predisposition and poor socialisation rather than wider structural inequality.

questions.q: Liberal feminism is distinctive in arguing that gender inequality can be reduced mainly through:
options: The violent overthrow of patriarchy
Abolishing the capitalist economy first
Rejecting any idea of progress
Gradual reform, legal change and challenging gender socialisation
questions.explain: Liberal feminists believe equality can be achieved progressively through legal reform, equal opportunities and changing socialisation.

questions.q: In labelling theory, a 'master status' refers to:
options: A label such as 'criminal' that overrides all other statuses a person holds
The official crime rate published by the state
The dominant value system of the ruling class
The highest rank within a criminal organisation
questions.explain: Once labelled a criminal, this becomes a master status that controls how others perceive the individual above all their other identities.

questions.q: Jock Young's left realist 'square of crime' relates the offender, the state, the public and which other element?
options: The media
The church
The school
The victim
questions.explain: The square of crime relates the offender, victim, state agencies and the wider society/public to understand crime fully.

questions.q: Albert Cohen's concept of 'status frustration' explains delinquency as a result of:
options: Excessive media coverage of youth crime
An inherited criminal gene passed between generations
Working-class boys failing in a middle-class school system and inverting its values
The chivalry of the police towards male offenders
questions.explain: Cohen argued that boys denied status in mainstream society form delinquent subcultures that invert mainstream values to gain status among peers.

questions.q: Right realism, associated with Wilson and Kelling's 'broken windows' thesis, recommends:
options: Reducing all forms of surveillance
Maintaining order through zero-tolerance policing of minor disorder
Abolishing prisons entirely
Tackling the root social causes of poverty
questions.explain: The broken windows thesis argues that swiftly addressing minor signs of disorder prevents an area from spiralling into serious crime.

questions.q: Max Weber argued that a full sociological explanation of action requires both causal explanation and:
options: The abandonment of objectivity
The complete rejection of statistics
A focus only on the economic base
'Verstehen', an empathetic understanding of the actor's subjective meaning
questions.explain: Weber combined structural causes with Verstehen, the interpretive understanding of the meanings actors give to their behaviour.

questions.q: In Merton's typology of adaptations, an 'innovator' is someone who:
options: Rejects both the goals and the means
Accepts the goals but uses illegitimate means to achieve them
Accepts the means but abandons the goals
Withdraws from society altogether
questions.explain: Innovators accept the cultural goal of success but turn to illegitimate means, such as theft, when legitimate routes are blocked.

questions.q: Cloward and Ohlin identified three types of deviant subculture. Which subculture emerges where there is no organised criminal opportunity structure?
options: The retreatist subculture
The criminal subculture
The conflict subculture
The conformist subculture
questions.explain: The conflict subculture arises in disorganised areas lacking a stable criminal hierarchy, channelling frustration into gang violence over territory.

questions.q: A laboratory experiment is rarely used in sociology mainly because:
options: It produces no quantitative data
It is impossible to control any variables
It is favoured by interpretivists
It is artificial, can only study small groups, and raises ethical and validity problems
questions.explain: Lab experiments struggle with the artificiality of settings, the Hawthorne effect and ethics, limiting their use in studying real social life.

questions.q: Parsons compared society to a biological organism. In this analogy, social institutions are like:
options: Interdependent organs each meeting a functional need of the whole
Isolated cells with no connection
Competing predators
Random external shocks
questions.explain: Parsons' organic analogy treats institutions as interdependent parts that each contribute to the survival and equilibrium of the social system.

questions.q: Stanley Cohen's study of Mods and Rockers introduced which key concept?
options: Folk devils and moral panics
The square of crime
The chivalry thesis
Anomie
questions.explain: Cohen showed how the media constructed Mods and Rockers as 'folk devils', triggering a moral panic that amplified deviance.

questions.q: The New Right perspective on sociology and social policy typically argues that:
options: Capitalism is the sole cause of crime
Sociology should never influence policy
State welfare should be expanded to eliminate poverty
Generous welfare creates a 'dependency culture' and undermines self-reliance
questions.explain: New Right thinkers such as Murray argue over-generous welfare fosters dependency and an underclass, favouring reduced state intervention.

questions.q: Situational crime prevention, associated with Clarke, focuses primarily on:
options: Eliminating relative deprivation
Reforming the offender's personality through therapy
Reducing opportunities for crime by 'target hardening' the environment
Increasing media coverage of crime
questions.explain: Situational crime prevention seeks to design out crime by making targets harder to attack, though critics note it can simply displace crime.

questions.q: Symbolic interactionism, associated with Mead and Blumer, holds that:
options: Behaviour is wholly determined by social structures
People act towards things on the basis of the meanings those things have for them
Only quantitative data reveals social reality
Society exists independently of human interaction
questions.explain: Interactionists argue that meaning is created and negotiated through interaction, and that the self develops through taking the role of others.

questions.q: Gouldner criticised value-free sociology by arguing that:
options: All sociology is naturally objective
Values are irrelevant to research
Only positivism can be value-laden
Claiming to be value-free can mask a conservative bias and a sale of expertise to the powerful
questions.explain: Gouldner argued that a supposedly value-free sociology often serves established interests, and that committed sociology is preferable.

questions.q: 'State crime', as analysed by sociologists such as Green and Ward, refers to:
options: Illegal or deviant acts committed by, or with the complicity of, state agencies
Petty theft in public buildings
Crime committed against the state by terrorists
Crime reported in state-owned newspapers
questions.explain: State crime includes genocide, torture and corruption carried out or sanctioned by governments, often on a vast scale.

questions.q: The practical, ethical and theoretical (PET) factors affecting choice of method include which practical consideration?
options: The time, funding and access available to the researcher
Informed consent of participants
The validity of the data
The researcher's theoretical perspective
questions.explain: Practical factors include time, money, funding, access to subjects and the personal characteristics of the researcher.

questions.q: According to Cloward and Ohlin, the 'retreatist subculture' is composed largely of:
options: Violent gang members fighting over turf
Police informants
Organised professional criminals
Those who fail in both legitimate and illegitimate opportunity structures, often turning to drug use
questions.explain: Retreatists are 'double failures' who cannot succeed legitimately or in crime and so retreat into drug use and other escapism.

questions.q: In participant observation, a key advantage claimed by interpretivists is:
options: The complete absence of ethical issues
The production of large statistical samples
High reliability and easy replication
High validity through first-hand insight into the group's meanings and way of life
questions.explain: Participant observation offers valid, in-depth understanding of a group from the inside, though it is hard to replicate and may raise ethics issues.

questions.q: The positivist position on whether sociology can be a science holds that:
options: Society cannot be measured objectively at all
Only empathetic understanding reveals truth
Science and sociology are entirely incompatible
Sociology can use scientific methods to discover observable, quantifiable social facts and causal laws
questions.explain: Positivists like Durkheim argued that sociology can study observable social facts objectively and uncover law-like causal patterns.

questions.q: According to Merton's strain theory, deviance arises primarily from:
options: A gap between culturally approved goals and the legitimate means to achieve them
The labelling of individuals by powerful agents
A lack of religious belief in society
An inborn biological disposition to break rules
questions.explain: Merton argued strain occurs when individuals cannot achieve shared cultural goals such as wealth through legitimate institutionalised means.

questions.q: Thomas Kuhn's concept of a 'paradigm' suggests that a discipline is a mature science when:
options: It is dominated by a single accepted framework that guides 'normal science'
Its findings are always subjective
It cannot be falsified
It rejects all shared assumptions
questions.explain: Kuhn argued a science is unified by a paradigm of shared assumptions; on this basis some claim sociology is 'pre-paradigmatic'.

questions.q: Howard Becker's labelling theory argues that deviance is best understood as:
options: The consequence of applying rules and sanctions to an 'offender'
A product of inadequate socialisation alone
A purely biological phenomenon
A quality inherent in the act itself
questions.explain: Becker argued deviance is not the act but the successful application of the deviant label by others to a person.

questions.q: Pat Carlen's study of women and crime emphasised that female offending is linked to:
options: The chivalry of male judges
Excessive media exposure
An innate maternal instinct to nurture
A failure of the 'class deal' and the 'gender deal' to deliver rewards
questions.explain: Carlen argued women turn to crime when the rewards promised by the class deal (work) and gender deal (family) fail to materialise.

questions.q: Giddens' 'structuration theory' attempts to resolve the structure-action debate by arguing that:
options: Structure and action are entirely separate
Only structure matters
Structure and agency are a 'duality': structures both constrain action and are reproduced by it
Only agency matters
questions.explain: Giddens argued structure and agency are two sides of the same process, as people draw on structures to act and thereby reproduce or change them.

questions.q: Frances Heidensohn argued that women commit less recorded crime than men largely because:
options: The police always ignore female crime
They are biologically more passive
They have higher levels of intelligence
Patriarchal control in the home, public space and work restricts their opportunities to offend
questions.explain: Heidensohn argued women are more controlled across domestic, public and workplace spheres, reducing their opportunities for crime.

questions.q: The concept of 'hegemonic masculinity', used by Messerschmidt, suggests that some men commit crime to:
options: Conform to feminist values
Gain leniency from the courts
Reduce relative deprivation in women
Express and accomplish a culturally dominant form of masculinity
questions.explain: Messerschmidt argued crime can be a resource for 'doing' masculinity when legitimate means of asserting it are unavailable.
